Idioms.phrase: Baby boomer - Someone born during the years following World War II.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Linda was born a few years after WWII, so she is part of the baby boomer generation. She's always talking about how she's a baby boomer.

Idioms.phrase: Backseat driver - A passenger who tries to interfere with the driver's driving.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Tammy always gets very irritated with backseat drivers. She can't understand why they won't just trust her to drive well!

Idioms.phrase: Back to basics - To go back to thinking about the basic elements of something.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, This issue seems to have become quite complex. Let's just try to go back to basics, so that we can better understand it.

Idioms.phrase: Back to square one - Back to the beginning of an endeavor.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Everything has gone wrong with the project! We have to go back to square one.

Idioms.phrase: Back to the drawing board – After experiencing failure, it's time to start a task over from scratch.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Ashley and her co-workers realized their first attempt at the task had been unsuccessful and they needed to go back to the drawing board.

Idioms.phrase: Backhanded compliment - A compliment that is really meant as an insult.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Can you believe how rude she was? She gave me such a backhanded compliment. She said that it's hard to be as beautiful as she is, and she would rather just be sweetly pretty like I am. She was definitely implying that I'm not as attractive as she is.

Idioms.phrase: Bad blood - Ill or negative feelings.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, There is quite a bit of bad blood between them now. They used to be friends, but a lot has happened to cause anger between them.

Idioms.phrase: Bad hair day - Hair is not looking as good as one would like.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Zack said he was having a very bad hair day. It was sticking up all over the place and he couldn't seem to tame it!

Idioms.phrase: Band-Aid on a bullet wound - Trying to deal with a serious situation in a negligent way.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Linda was amazed at the bad advice her cousin gave her on how to deal with the serious problem she was experiencing. It would be like putting a Band-Aid on a bullet wound.

Idioms.phrase: Barking up the wrong tree - To be searching for solutions in the wrong places.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I'm afraid you're barking up the wrong tree. I can't help you with your problem.

Idioms.phrase: Batting a thousand - To accomplish a task perfectly. A term taken from baseball.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Melissa knew that she was batting a thousand when she wrote the quiz. She knew the answer to every question.

Idioms.phrase: Be my guest - Go ahead.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I tried to get him to agree but wasn't successful. If you want to make an attempt, be my guest.

Idioms.phrase: Bear in mind/keep in mind - Remember something, especially while thinking about something else.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, It's true that we lost the game, but keep in mind that the other team cheated.

Idioms.phrase: Beat a hasty retreat - To leave really quickly, especially to flee a difficult situation.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Ethan and Michael jumped out of their seats when they realized how tricky the situation had become. They beat a hasty retreat.

Idioms.phrase: Beat around the bush - Trying to avoid saying something directly, often because the truth is uncomfortable.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Don't beat around the bush! Just tell me what you want to say.

Idioms.phrase: Beat someone to the draw - You do something before someone else manages to.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Joshua was determined to practice hard and beat his brother to the draw when it came to getting on a baseball team.

Idioms.phrase: Beat someone to the punch - To accomplish something before someone else does.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I'm so frustrated! I thought I was the first one to think of this idea, but it turned out that Mason beat me to the punch!

Idioms.phrase: Beat the bushes - To search thoroughly.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, She said she simply can't find her tablet. She claimed that she beat the bushes looking for it and there's just no sign of it.

Idioms.phrase: Beating a dead horse - Continuing to talk about a subject that is now useless to discuss.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Matthew kept talking about the subject and nobody knew why. Beating a dead horse like that was pointless.

Idioms.phrase: Beating around the bush - Trying to avoid a topic.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, No more beating around the bush! Tell me exactly what I need to know.

Idioms.phrase: Bed head - Hair that is messy after sleeping on it.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I had really bad bed head this morning. My hair was sticking up all over the place when I got up to brush my teeth!

Idioms.phrase: Bed of roses - A blissfully happy and comfortable situation.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, It's a good job, but don't expect it to be a bed of roses. It's quite difficult in many ways.

Idioms.phrase: Before you know it - Very soon.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The town is only about fifteen minutes away by car. We'll be there before you know it.

Idioms.phrase: Behind someone's back - Without someone knowing.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Max went behind my back and told people my secret. I'm really upset and don't know if we can be friends anymore.

Idioms.phrase: Behind the eight ball - In a difficult position or unfavorable circumstances.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I feel like I'm behind the eight ball here. These are really tricky circumstances.

Idioms.phrase: Belt and suspenders - Exercising caution and avoiding of risks.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Brian is a very cautious person. He avoids risks whenever possible. Belts and suspenders is his motto.

Idioms.phrase: Bend over backward - Try extremely hard to do something, usually to help someone with a specific issue.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, They bent over backward to help me learn this. I will always appreciate the effort they made.

Idioms.phrase: Bent out of shape - Annoyed and upset.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, There's no need to get so bent out of shape! I didn't say anything that you should be very angry about.

Idioms.phrase: Beside oneself - Very troubled or anxious and distraught.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Alexander was beside himself. He was so incredibly upset about his uncle's illness. His uncle had always been like a father to him.

Idioms.phrase: Beside the point – Irrelevant.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, They dismissed what I said, claiming that it was beside the point. They had already concluded the discussion.

Idioms.phrase: Bestie - Best friend.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, We're really good friends. She's my bestie, actually.

Idioms.phrase: Bet the ranch - To risk everything on an endeavor that you believe will be successful.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I tried to convince David to think more carefully about what he was doing. It's very dangerous to bet the ranch in that way. He could lose everything.

Idioms.phrase: Better late than never - It's preferable to do a thing late than to never do it.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, It took me a long time to get there, but better late than never!

Idioms.phrase: Between a rock and a hard place - Having to choose between two inadequate options when in a difficult situation.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Sean's friends can't understand why he hasn't been able to make a decision yet, but when you look at his options his hesitation is clear. Neither of them are good; he's between a rock and a hard place.

Idioms.phrase: Between the devil and the deep blue sea - Having to deal with the reality of two difficult possible outcomes for the same situation.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I think we're between the devil and the deep blue sea in this situation. No matter what we do, it's not going to solve the problem!

Idioms.phrase: Beyond the pale - Outside of the limits of socially or morally acceptable behavior.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The way they acted was truly beyond the pale. It was simply unacceptable. Don't you agree?

Idioms.phrase: Big cheese - A very important person, especially the most important person in an organization.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The boss is the big cheese in our company. She's the person who decides what gets done.

Idioms.phrase: Big fish in a small pond - Someone who seems more significant than they are because they live in a small or relatively insignificant community.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Mr. Jones is always so arrogant at social events. He and his family are important in their little town. They're big fish in a small pond.

Idioms.phrase: Big shot - A powerful person. Often used in a sarcastic or resentful way.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Marvin thinks he's a big shot. He thinks he's better than us and can tell us what to do.

Idioms.phrase: Big wheel - An influential, powerful, and important person.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, He's a big wheel in this organization. Whatever he says goes.

Idioms.phrase: Bigger bang for your buck - More value for money.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The salesperson directed me to a fridge different from the one I had originally wanted to buy. He claimed that it offered better features and bigger bang for my buck.

Idioms.phrase: Bigwig - A powerful person with a high position in a corporate structure.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Everyone knows that the CEO is the most important bigwig in any company.

Idioms.phrase: Bird's-eye view - A broad and expansive view of a place or something.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The helicopter ride was a lot of fun! We got a bird's-eye view of the entire town!

Idioms.phrase: Birds of a feather flock together - Friends are often alike (usually used in a negative sense).
Idioms.definition: As in this example, They weren't surprised that the group of friends exhibited similar personalities. After all, birds of a feather flock together.

Idioms.phrase: Bite off more than you can chew - To take on a task that you're unable to finish.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, We weren't surprised when Barbara and Matthew couldn't finish the task. They'd bitten off more than they could chew.

Idioms.phrase: Bite the bullet - To commence with something that is unpleasant, but inevitable.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, They decided to bite the bullet and go ahead with the necessary expense.

Idioms.phrase: Bite the dust - For something to cease to exist.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, My plans for vacation bit the dust when I found out that I'd only be getting one week off.

Idioms.phrase: Bite your tongue - To stop talking.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I was going to give my opinion on his outfit, but I decided to bite my tongue at the last minute. I didn't think he'd like what I had to say.

Idioms.phrase: Black and blue - To be bruised.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Christopher's knees were black and blue after falling off his bike a few days ago.

Idioms.phrase: Black-and-white - To think in an extreme way—everything is either completely right or entirely wrong
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Josh always seemed to take a black-and-white view of things. It was difficult to make him see that there could be gray areas.

Idioms.phrase: Black market - An illegal market of some sort.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The counterfeit goods market is illegal. It is a black market.

Idioms.phrase: Black sheep - To not fit in within a specific group.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, When she was growing up, Julia felt like she was the black sheep of her family. She was very rebellious and didn't feel like she fit in.

Idioms.phrase: Black tie event - A very formal event in which men must wear tuxedos and women wear formal gowns.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The banquet was a black tie event. That's why everyone wore tuxedos and gowns.

Idioms.phrase: Blackball someone - To cause someone to be rejected by workplaces or other establishments throughout a field in a certain location.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The actor realized that he'd been blackballed since he hadn't been able to get along with a certain director. He couldn’t get any new parts.

Idioms.phrase: Blast from the past - A vivid reminder of the past.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Did you see the old acid-washed jean jacket that Megan found in her closet yesterday? Talk about a blast from the past! I think I had one of those.

Idioms.phrase: Blaze a trail - To take a different and challenging path.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Emily was so daring and adventurous. She wasn't afraid of making unconventional choices and blazing a trail.

Idioms.phrase: Blew me away - Incredibly impressed me.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Yes, we went to the movie last night. It really blew me away! I thought it was incredible.

Idioms.phrase: Blonde bombshell - An extremely beautiful and glamorous woman with blonde (probably light blonde) hair.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Many of the actresses of the 1940s and ’50s were called blonde bombshells. Marilyn Monroe is certainly the most famous.

Idioms.phrase: Blow a fuse - To lose one's temper.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, My friend blew a fuse the other day when I found fault with their work. I guess I don't really blame them for getting angry.

Idioms.phrase: Blow off steam - To vent energy, frustration, or anger.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I have had a very stressful week and I'm hoping to blow off some steam this Saturday. I'll be playing baseball with my team.

Idioms.phrase: Blow one's top - To lose one's temper.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, They were afraid that she would blow her top when she heard the news. It was just the kind of thing that could make her angry.

Idioms.phrase: Blowing smoke - Exaggerating and/or making false claims about oneself, most often to make oneself look better.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Richard was known for boasting about his accomplishments. People thought he was just blowing smoke.

Idioms.phrase: Blue blood - To be a member of the aristocracy or a royal family. In the American context, this can apply to people who belong to old and famous families with a great deal of wealth.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The family considered themselves blue blood, but I didn't think they were as distinguished as they thought.

Idioms.phrase: Blue law - A law meant to regulate personal behavior (for example, gambling or seeing a certain movie).
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I didn't realize that this state had any blue laws. Not being allowed to gamble is unusual.

Idioms.phrase: Boiling point - The point at which someone becomes angry.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I think I'm starting to reach my boiling point! They're making me so mad!

Idioms.phrase: Bolt from the blue - Something that occurs without any warning and is a total surprise.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Hearing the news caught us off guard. It was really a bolt from the blue.

Idioms.phrase: Bone of contention - A source of conflict or disagreement.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The major bone of contention was the question of whether or not Jonah and James should be in charge of the project. No one could agree and people were debating each man's merits.

Idioms.phrase: Bookworm - Someone who reads books very frequently, or almost all of the time.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I'm definitely a bookworm. I love to read and do so whenever I get the chance.

Idioms.phrase: Born with a silver spoon in one's mouth - To be born into a wealthy family with lots of privileges.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Zoe always had lots of designer clothes and expensive jewelry when she was a kid. She was born with a silver spoon in her mouth.

Idioms.phrase: Bottom of the barrel - The lowest quality option.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Wow! They were really scraping the bottom of the barrel with this. They're using their last option.

Idioms.phrase: Boxed in - To feel trapped in some way.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, James felt boxed in with the situation. He didn't feel he had any real options.

Idioms.phrase: Brainstorm - To come up with as many ideas as possible.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The team at the office brainstormed to come up with ideas for the new venture.

Idioms.phrase: Bread and butter - A job or endeavor that allows someone to make a living.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Abigail does several different kinds of work, but tutoring is her bread and butter.

Idioms.phrase: Break a leg - A wish of good luck, especially in a performance.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, You're starring in a play tonight? That's amazing! Well, break a leg!

Idioms.phrase: Break even - To neither gain nor lose money.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Patrick is worried about his investment, thinking it might have been unwise. He'd be happy and relieved just to break even.

Idioms.phrase: Break someone's heart - To romantically disappoint someone who is in love with you.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, He was afraid of telling her his real feelings in case he broke her heart.

Idioms.phrase: Break the bank - For something to cost a huge amount of money.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I'm glad to hear about our upcoming vacation to Hawaii. Aren't you worried that it might break the bank, though?

Idioms.phrase: Break the ice - Do something to help new acquaintances feel more comfortable
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Things were awkward at the party until we played a game to help break the ice.

Idioms.phrase: Break the news - To tell someone (or a group of people) news about something.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, It took her a while to get up the courage to break the news about what had happened.

Idioms.phrase: Breeze through - To get through something with very little or no effort.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Abby breezed through the course. She found it very easy and it didn't take a great deal of effort.

Idioms.phrase: Bright and early - Early in the morning.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Remember to wake up bright and early tomorrow. There's a lot to do.

Idioms.phrase: Bring down the house - To be extremely successful, usually in a performance.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The cast brought down the house with last night's performance. They were amazing and got a standing ovation!

Idioms.phrase: Bring home the bacon - To earn most, or all, of the money an individual or family needs.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Her best friend told her there's no shame in any honest job, as long as it lets you bring home the bacon.

Idioms.phrase: Bring my A game - To make my best effort.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I promised my friends that I'd bring my A game to the competition tomorrow, so I need to get lots of sleep.

Idioms.phrase: Brought up - To begin speaking on a topic.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, He brought up a topic I didn't want to discuss. I explained that I just didn't want to have a conversation about that today.

Idioms.phrase: Brownie points - To earn Brownie points is to be good and kind to others. Brownie refers to the Brownies, a club for kids.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Kate is always kind and helpful to everyone. And she's so honest, too. She's always earning her Brownie points!

Idioms.phrase: Bull in a china shop - To be clumsy and perhaps oafish when a more delicate approach is needed.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Walt didn't know how to act in a delicate situation. He was like a bull in a china shop.

Idioms.phrase: Burgers and dogs - Hamburgers and hotdogs (a hotdog is a sausage made of a meat such as pork or beef in a bread bun).
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Come to my picnic next week! We're having some burgers and dogs.

Idioms.phrase: Burn bridges - To ruin relationships.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Paul was considered very unreliable by everyone. He was known for burning bridges and ruining friendships.

Idioms.phrase: Burn the candle at both ends - To live a frantic sort of life, going to bed too late and having to wake up too early, thus not getting enough rest.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I'm worried about Tim. I think he's burning the candle at both ends. He doesn't get enough rest and always seems worried and frantic.

Idioms.phrase: Burn the midnight oil - To continue working late into the night. This is a reference to long ago when people didn't have electric light.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Evan and Elsie are still working on their school assignment and it's well past three o'clock in the morning. They're really burning the midnight oil!

Idioms.phrase: Burned out - To feel exhausted as the result of a specific endeavor.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, William felt burned out from his job. He was too tired to think and felt like he couldn't deal with anything else.

Idioms.phrase: Bury the hatchet - To let go of a disagreement or grudge and call a truce.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, They have been friends for a long time. When they fought a few weeks ago, they ended up not talking for several days. They eventually decided to make up and bury the hatchet, though.

Idioms.phrase: Bury your head in the sand - Pretending something doesn't exist, or completely ignoring it.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, I know you're having a difficult time with the situation but burying your head in the sand isn't going to help make the problem go away.

Idioms.phrase: Busy bee - Someone who always seems to be busy.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Louise is definitely a busy bee. She's always running around, getting things done.

Idioms.phrase: Butter someone up - To flatter and be excessively nice to someone, in an attempt to make them see things your way or do something you want.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, His parents still haven't said that he's allowed to go. He's still trying to butter them up.

Idioms.phrase: Button one's lip - To stop talking and be quiet.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, The teacher told her pupil to button his lip while she was talking. He was trying to interrupt her.

Idioms.phrase: Buy a lemon - To buy a car that ends up being highly faulty or non-functioning.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, He was so excited to buy his second-hand car, but it ended up being a lemon! He's going to have to spend a fortune on repairs and even then it still might give him trouble.

Idioms.phrase: Buy something for a song - To buy something for very little money.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Do you like my new coat? I got it for a song! It was on sale.

Idioms.phrase: By hook or by crook - No matter what, or by any means.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, Don't worry about it. By hook or by crook, we’ll definitely find a way to get the job done.

Idioms.phrase: By the book - Strictly following the rules.
Idioms.definition: As in this example, They always do everything by the book. They follow the rules meticulously.
